extraction.name: MMMU
extraction.description: A massive multi-discipline multimodal understanding and reasoning benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal models on college-level tasks requiring expert-level perception, domain knowledge, and deliberate reasoning. It includes 11.5K multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks across six disciplines, 30 subjects, 183 subfields, and 30 image types.
extraction.creator: Xiang Yue, Yuansheng Ni, Kai Zhang, Tianyu Zheng, Ruoqi Liu, Ge Zhang, Samuel Stevens, Dongfu Jiang, Weiming Ren, Yuxuan Sun, Cong Wei, Botao Yu, Ruibin Yuan, Renliang Sun, Ming Yin, Boyuan Zheng, Zhenzhu Yang, Yibo Liu, Wenhao Huang, Huan Sun, Yu Su, Wenhu Chen
extraction.citeAs: Yue, Xiang, et al. "MMMU: A Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark for Expert AGI." arXiv:2311.16502v4, 2024.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The benchmark collection takes three stages. First, the authors went through common university majors to decide which subjects to include, selecting 30 subjects from six disciplines based on whether visual inputs are commonly adopted. Second, they recruited over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in these majors as annotators to collect multimodal questions from major textbooks and online resources, and to create new questions based on their expertise where necessary. Annotators were instructed to adhere to copyright and license regulations and to avoid sources prohibiting copy and redistribution. To reduce data contamination concerns, annotators were advised to select questions without immediately available answers, such as those with answers in separate documents or at the end of textbooks. This process resulted in a diverse collection of 13K questions from various sources. The final benchmark contains 11.5K carefully selected questions after quality control and filtering.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Document analysis, Secondary Data analysis, Others
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Questions were drawn from free online resources, quizzes, textbooks, lecture materials, and other study materials, including college exams, quizzes, and textbooks.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Data quality control involved three stages: lexical overlap and source URL similarity were used to identify potential duplicate problems, which were then reviewed by the authors to eliminate duplications; problems were distributed among co-authors for format and typo checking to ensure adherence to a standardized format; and authors categorized problems into four difficulty levels, after which approximately 10% classified as very easy were excluded from the benchmark.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: All questions were required to contain one or more images, be written in English, meet college-level difficulty, and be answerable with one of the given options or a short answer. Questions were clearly categorized as multiple-choice or open-ended. Annotators labeled fields including question text, answer options, correct answer, image types, question difficulty, and explanation if available. The structured format used separate JSON files per sample, with images inserted as file paths in questions, options, or explanations.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in the selected majors served as annotators to collect and author questions. The annotation protocol specified that data be primarily collected from free online resources, quizzes, textbooks, and other study materials; that questions include one or more images; be in English; be college-level; and be non-ambiguous. Annotators categorized each question as multiple-choice or open-ended and annotated question text, answer options, correct answer, image types, question difficulty, and explanation if available. Ambiguous instances were flagged for detailed review in team meetings. A secondary review team rigorously vetted annotations, and regular audits of random samples were conducted.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: A user-friendly web interface for data annotation and verification
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Potential duplicate problems were identified using lexical overlap and source URL similarity and then reviewed by authors. Problems were checked for format and typos, categorized into four difficulty levels, and very easy questions were excluded. Ambiguous or unclear instances were flagged for collaborative review in team meetings to establish a standardized annotation approach. The paper also notes 2% annotation error in GPT-4V error analysis.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in the selected majors and disciplines; 50 college students from various disciplines and subjects are also described as manually collecting the questions.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The appendix includes a version change log. Changes are documented from V1 (Nov. 27) to V2 (Dec. 18), V3 (Dec. 21), and V4 (June. 13). The lead author took the lead in the dataset release. The live-updating leaderboard is available at the project website.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The annotation protocol instructs annotators to avoid collecting questions that contain any private information.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark is motivated by monitoring progress toward Expert AGI, which the paper links to significant societal importance because such systems could reach a substitution threshold for human labor in many industries, leading to risks of job displacement and economic disruption. The authors believe MMMU will help develop next-generation multimodal foundation models and monitor progress toward Expert AGI.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper states that MMMU, like any benchmark, has limitations and that the manual curation process may carry biases. It also notes that GPT-4V often exhibits a bias towards text, prioritizing textual information over visual inputs.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The authors caution that MMMU is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI because there is no direct mapping between performance on MMMU and the 90th percentile of skilled adults, and college exams are not the only tasks an AGI should tackle. They also note that the manual curation process may carry biases and that the focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is a benchmark for evaluating multimodal models on expert-level multimodal understanding and reasoning. It is divided into a few-shot development set, a validation set useful for hyperparameter selection, and a test set. The paper evaluates models in zero-shot settings and also reports few-shot results for some models in the appendix.
